tasks.title: Simulator: bring up an oVirt data center
tasks.statement: Build an oVirt environment the way an administrator does in the Administration Portal: a cluster, hosts, the logical network vm-net, a storage domain and a virtual machine. Every object has its own states and the order of actions matters: a domain is created by a host in Up status, the data center comes alive only after the master domain is activated, and a network that is required in the cluster makes hosts without it NonOperational. The exercise is solved when all three goals are met.
tasks.hint: Start with the cluster and a host. The vm-net network makes hosts without it NonOperational — assign it to their NICs. A domain takes three steps: create, attach, activate. For a host to go into maintenance, the virtual machine needs another host with its network.

tasks.title: Board: assemble an oVirt environment
tasks.statement: On the board you assemble an oVirt environment: add the engine, data centers, clusters, hosts, logical networks, storage domains and virtual machines, and connect them. The statuses follow from the links: a host without a required network is NonOperational, a host without a management network to the engine is NonResponsive, a data center without an active master domain is not Up. The “Message path” buttons show how an engine command travels over the networks and where it breaks. Assemble or repair the environment in five scenarios. The exercise is solved when the goals of all scenarios are met.
tasks.hint: A link goes from the output of one object to the input of another: engine → data center → cluster → host. A network is defined in the data center, attached to the cluster and assigned to every host, and the engine needs a NIC in the management network. A storage domain is attached to the data center and then connected to every host. Click an object to see the reason for its status.

tasks.title: Board: clusters and placement
tasks.statement: Build an oVirt environment on the board: clusters, hosts, networks and VMs. Five scenarios: place VMs on hosts so that each can be migrated; attach a network to all three clusters; move a host from one cluster to another; put a cluster that is outside any data center into one; move a cluster to another data center. The exercise is solved when every scenario is solved.
tasks.hint: A cluster is the border of live migration, a data center is the border of networks and storage. Select an object to read the reason for its status.

tasks.title: Board: hierarchy puzzles
tasks.statement: Five puzzles on one board: an environment without an engine, a network in the wrong data center, a VM with a foreign disk, three data centers with a broken path from the engine, and an environment with three independent faults. Read the reasons of the statuses and follow the path of a command. The exercise is solved when every scenario is solved.
tasks.hint: Go from the symptom to the cause: the status of an object, its reason, the link of the hierarchy that is missing.

tasks.title: Where a machine runs
tasks.statement: The oVirt inventory is nested dictionaries: data center → cluster → host → list of virtual machine names, for example {"dc1": {"cl1": {"h1": ["web", "db"]}}}. Write a function vm_path(inventory, vm): return a string like "dc1/cl1/h1" for the host where the machine vm runs, or an empty string if there is no such machine.
tasks.hint: Three nested loops over items(); once you find the name in the list, build the path.

tasks.title: Inventory counters
tasks.statement: For the inventory from the previous task (data center → cluster → host → list of VMs) write a function inventory_stats(inventory): return a tuple of four numbers: how many data centers, clusters, hosts, and virtual machines the inventory has.
tasks.hint: Accumulate four counters in the same nested loops.

tasks.title: Cluster CPU baseline
tasks.statement: A cluster's CPU type cannot be newer than its oldest host. You get generations, the names of processor generations from old to new, for example ["Nehalem", "Sandy Bridge", "Haswell", "Skylake"], and host_cpus, the generations of the cluster's hosts. Write a function cluster_baseline(generations, host_cpus): return the oldest generation among the hosts. If there are no hosts, return an empty string.
tasks.hint: A generation's rank is generations.index(name); take the minimum by that key.

tasks.title: REST request URL
tasks.statement: The engine's REST interface lives at https://<host>/ovirt-engine/api. Write a function api_url(host, path, query): path is a string like "vms/123/start" (it may have extra slashes at the start and end, strip them), query is a dictionary of parameters. Return the full URL; add the parameters after a ? sorted by name and joined with &, as name=value (values are strings or numbers, no escaping needed). An empty query gives a URL without ?; an empty path gives the API root without a trailing slash.
tasks.hint: Use path.strip('/'); if it is empty, add no slash. For parameters use sorted(query.items()).

tasks.title: Host states
tasks.statement: A simplified model of a host's life. Transitions (state, event) → new state: (Maintenance, activate) → Up; (Up, maintenance) → PreparingForMaintenance; (PreparingForMaintenance, vms_migrated) → Maintenance; (Up, no_heartbeat) → NonResponsive; (NonResponsive, heartbeat) → Up; (NonResponsive, fenced) → Reboot; (Reboot, heartbeat) → Up. Any event with no transition leaves the state unchanged. Write a function final_state(start, events): return the state after all the events in order.
tasks.hint: Put the transitions into a dictionary keyed by a tuple and use table.get((state, event), state).

tasks.title: Compatibility version
tasks.statement: Versions are written as strings like "4.7" (the major and minor parts are integers and must be compared as numbers, so "4.10" is newer than "4.9"). A cluster can be moved to a new version target if three conditions hold: target is not lower than the cluster's current version current, target is not higher than the data center's version dc, and target is not higher than the weakest host supports (host_max is a list of the hosts' maximum versions). Write a function can_upgrade(current, target, dc, host_max): return True or False.
tasks.hint: Turn a version into a tuple of numbers: tuple(map(int, s.split('.'))); tuples compare the way you need.

tasks.title: Which ports are missing
tasks.statement: For the platform to work, a host must have these ports open: 22 (SSH), 54321 (VDSM), 16514 (libvirt over TLS) and the range 49152–49215 for migration. Write a function missing_ports(open_ports): open_ports is a list of open numbers and ranges (a range is a tuple (from, to) inclusive). Return a sorted list of the missing required ports from the first three; the migration range counts as closed unless a single open range covers it entirely, in which case add its start 49152 to the answer as a marker. A single open port inside the migration range does not cover the range.
tasks.hint: For each required port, check whether it equals a number in the list or lies in some tuple. For the migration range, one tuple covering 49152..49215 is enough.

tasks.title: Host score for the hosted engine
tasks.statement: Hosted-engine services choose the host with the best score for the engine. A simplified model based on the hosted-engine agent's settings: the score starts at 3400; if the gateway is unreachable, subtract 1600; if there is no management network (the management bridge), subtract 600; if free memory is below 4096 MB (the threshold is a value of our model), subtract 400; the CPU penalty grows linearly: zero up to 40 percent load, 1000 from 90 percent, and (load − 40) * 20 in between. The score is never below zero. Write a function best_host(hosts): hosts is a dictionary name → dictionary with the fields gateway (bool), mgmt (bool), free_mb (a number), cpu (percent). Return the name of the host with the highest score; on a tie, the alphabetically smaller name. For an empty dictionary, return an empty string.
tasks.hint: Write a separate function score(h) and sort by (-score, name).

tasks.title: Host order for placement
tasks.statement: A simplified scheduler places a new machine on the least loaded host of the cluster. You get an inventory (data center → cluster → host → list of VMs) and a cluster name cluster (cluster names are unique across the inventory). Write a function placement_order(inventory, cluster): return the list of the cluster's host names sorted by VM count ascending, and by name on a tie. If there is no such cluster, return an empty list.
tasks.hint: Find the cluster's host dictionary in two loops, then sorted(hosts, key=lambda h: (len(hosts[h]), h)).

tasks.title: Where the time went
tasks.statement: A machine-start command passes the links engine → vdsm → libvirt → qemu. The trace log is a list of tuples (link, start, end) in seconds; the links are nested, so a link's own time is its duration minus the duration of the next link in the log (the last link counts in full). Write a function slowest_link(trace): return the name of the link with the largest own time; on a tie, the one that comes earlier in the log. For an empty log, return an empty string.
tasks.hint: Duration = end − start; the own time of link i = duration i minus duration i+1.
